abstract: Attempts to determine the function of microglia activation and the immune system in neurodegenerative diseases have yielded conflicting results, with some data showing a protective effect, while other data shows a detrimental effect. This discrepancy in the function of microglia activation and the immune system in neurodegeneration likely stems from differing functions during the build-up of pathological proteins versus later stage defects. Therefore, we investigated the function of microglia activation and the immune system in Lsd1 inducible deletion mice, which serve as a late-stage tau-associated neurodegeneration model without the build-up of pathological proteins. We found that loss of LSD1 causes the morphological and transcriptional activation of microglia, accompanied by astrocyte activation and a broader immune response. Blocking microglia activation by inactivating Trem2 inhibited the entire Lsd1-induced immune response, while pharmacologically inhibiting microglia via PLX3397 treatment eliminated microglia but did not block astrocyte reactivity or the broader immune response. Surprisingly, despite these effects, neither blocking microglia activation nor depleting microglia prevented Lsd1-induced neurodegeneration, paralysis and death. Instead, we found in both cases that survival was significantly reduced. These results suggest that microglia and microglial activation, independent of astrocyte reactivity and the broader inflammatory response, is neuroprotective in a late-stage tau-associated neurodegeneration model.
